newsitem.title: UK: UK's Major makes moral case for lower taxation.
newsitem.headline: UK's Major makes moral case for lower taxation.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major, setting out a moral as well as an economic case for smaller government, recommitted his government on Wednesday to eventually abolishing capital gains and inheritance taxes.
In the annual lecture of the right-wing Spectator magazine, Major said his Conservative party's instinct for less government marked a sharp divide with the main opposition Labour party.
"We aim to tax and spend an even smaller share of what people earn. To reduce and, in due course, abolish capital taxation," Major said.
To do so made good economic sense because it would end a penalty on enterprise and investment, thus releasing capital and creating jobs.
"And that is the right thing to do. There is a moral case for low taxation if you genuinely want to see growing prosperity and more employment," the prime minister added.
He said "moral" was a word he usually preferred to leave to the Church, but it was apt.

"For example, is it moral to take from individuals the right to make personal decisions? Is it moral to impose obligations on employers like the Social Chapter and the minimum wage that will cost jobs and prevent those without jobs from getting them? Again, I think not.
"Is it moral to compulsorily take too much tax from people for government to spend and diminish individual choices? My answer is no," Major said.

An aide said Major felt it was sanctimonious and cynical for Labour to stake out the high moral ground in politics, and he wanted to explain why it was the Conservative commitment to slim government and personal responsibility that was in fact moral.
But Labour, seizing on Major's argument, said the fact that his government had raised taxes 22 times since 1992 demonstrated that "by any reasonable criteria he is morally bankrupt".
Major reaffirmed that he would look further at a lower target for public spending once it had been reduced to below 40 percent of nation income, from about 41 percent now.
In a theme that aides said would be amplified in the run-up to the election, he also signalled plans to extend freedom and choice: "Not for one class, not one faction, but all in society.

"Having built the strongest economy we've known for decades, we now need to turn to giving all in society the chance to take more control of their lives. Those living in Labour strongholds, just as much as those in leafy Conservative heartlands. They all matter just as much," the prime minister said.
